title: A Perfect Game
reviewNotes: Montages, captions and native complete diagrams reviewed. Native89 confirms the complete ten-piece final checked board after Ra7+: White Kc5/Ra7/b6/c4/f2/h3 against Kb7/Rf7/g7/g5, Black to move. Kc8 and Kb8 are the only legal replies. Independent Kc8/b7+/Kd8 demonstrates that b7+ does not force Kb8. Independent Kb8/Ra8+/Kxa8/b7+/Kb8 is legal but leaves a nine-piece position with the pawn blocked on b7 by Black Kb8: b8=Q is illegal while b8 is occupied. This is a comparison, not a recommended line or a recovered source score. Preserve both rooks until actual capture and all six pawns. The winner badge is not an exact conversion certificate. Verify every rook/king defense, pawn race and complete larger ending; previous eleven- and ten-piece drafts and review history remain preserved. Full board images/captions are available.
transcript: Fools will resign. Wise players might make a draw, but only a true genius would be able to win from this position. And yes, I am talking about the starting position of the game of chess. And that is exactly what I did at the Grenke Chess Festival, where I played a game at an accuracy of 97% and this was a 44 moves long game. So there was no cheap trick from the opening. We went into this line that I had studied before the tournament. My opponent had seen from the online database that I had two games in this position. One where the opponent played Queen b6 and after some brilliant moves, he had proceeded to win a comfortable end game for black. And another game where after these moves and I play Queen b3 first and we got this trade, I still lost that game pretty badly. But because I had played those games, I knew the plans so extremely well and I was so prepared that I played this game almost perfectly. And here my opponent actually blunders right away. This allows me to take the knight. You cannot take with the rook because of course I'm going to take like this, but if you take with the pawn, I have Bishop to a6 and my Bishop's crisscross applesauce this rook and so the rook is either trapped or it has to give up this pawn, which is what happened in the game. Now here are the only two inaccuracies of the entire game. I played a4 where the engine wanted me to attack the Bishop with g4 right away and I then decided right here to castle. And by the way, this was the only way that I found to play the line because if you take here after knight takes, there is a threat from black of trapping this Bishop and if I retreat the Bishop, black is going to win after takes, takes and picking up the rook and castling doesn't fix the issue because after rook here and Bishop to b5, you don't want to take the Bishop anymore because the rook is defended, but you can come here and now add more pressure to the file and if I move my Bishop away, now the pawn is going to fall like this. And the only way that I found to escape all of that was to play G4, push the bishop back, knight E5, and after F6, I can trade here. And after this entire line, if the same thing happens, castles, and rook here, and bishop here, and rook here, I now have bishop to D3 attacking an extra pawn. So, it doesn't matter that black wins a pawn back like this because I now run here. But instead of all of this, my opponent decided to trade the bishop for the knight. And now, we entered an end game where I am going to have a passed pawn. And so, I played B3 with intention of playing C4, which is why my opponent plays C4 himself. But this is a massive mistake. This allows me to take and bring the rook around defending the passed pawn. And now, with some precise end game technique, I brought my king around trying to pick up this pawn right here. It seems like I cannot come forward, but I have B6, rook B7, and rook B5 check, and now it's just over. I'm going to pick up the pawn and win this game smoothly and easily. And this is a reminder that winning tactically is not the only option. Positional chess is a thing.
